source.title: Quartet: Native FP4 Training Can Be Optimal for Large Language Models
source.authors: Roberto L. Castro; Andrei Panferov; Soroush Tabesh; Oliver Sieberling; Jiale Chen; Mahdi Nikdan; Saleh Ashkboos; Dan Alistarh

record.tranche_reason: The study fits and evaluates its own loss-scaling law across training precisions and data budgets. This bears directly on scaling-law claims, but its focus is quantized training rather than reproducing the original parameter/token/compute experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own C4 validation losses, scaling-law fits, and a downstream-performance comparison; these are recorded below. Claims about prior work in the related-work section are not recorded as results. Gradient-alignment measurements and kernel speedups are not rows because they do not measure the claimed loss-scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: Scaling laws are mainly a tool here, used to compare quantized training methods. The study does report its own results on the claim: a BF16 baseline fit of the parametric law (N 30M–200M, D/N 25–800 on C4) with fit errors, alternative-form fits shown against larger 430M/800M points, and a downstream-vs-loss correspondence plot. These bear weakly on V1, V2 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors propose comparing quantized training methods through their induced scaling laws (parameter and data efficiency). They report that Quartet (QuEST forward, RTN backward, MXFP4) beats prior 4-bit methods in loss and is near-lossless in the large-data regime. Its Blackwell kernels give about 1.6× training speedup over FP8, making MXFP4 training competitive with or optimal against FP8 on accuracy versus speed.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits a precision-dependent loss law and tests quantized Llama pretraining, rather than reproducing the original studies' parameter/token/compute scaling experiments or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted efficiency and observed loss depend on the quantization method; the paper reports distinct method-specific efficiency factors and substantially different validation losses, including instability for some methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Forward-pass and backward-pass precision enter the loss law as multiplicative efficiency factors on N and D. For example, effN is 0.42/0.59/0.64 for SR/RTN/QuEST, and Quartet has effN 0.65 and effD 0.95.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-precision training shifts the loss scaling law by reducing effective parameter count (forward precision) and effective data (backward precision).

record.problems: The directly tabulated quantized-method loss sweep is for 30M parameters; most larger-run comparisons are shown in figures without exact per-run values. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant loss comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only loss trajectories and gradient-quality measurements in Figures 1–2 were not extracted as separate rows because exact per-condition loss values are not stated and the gradient measures are not the claimed loss behavior. Figure 6 is represented by r2; larger-model points there are not reported as exact predicted-versus-observed losses.

untested.parts: Fit across several orders of magnitude in N; separate power laws in compute; scaling of N beyond 200M within the fit.
Quantitative accuracy of extrapolation to 430M/800M (figure only) and beyond.
No other modalities, repeated data or fine-tuning. Low-precision training is fitted only through efficiency factors, with no fit quality reported.
No quantitative predictability of downstream scores; only a qualitative correspondence plot.
The alternative fitted forms are shown, but differences in exponents or compute-optimal split across forms are not reported.

missing.what: Fit errors for the three alternative scaling-law forms (8.65e-06, 6.40e-06, 1.65e-06) and their extrapolation to 430M/800M points
Fitted effN/effD for Table 3 methods (Quartet 0.65/0.95; LUQ-INT4 0.49/0.15; others 'Unstable')

record.verdict_notes: Most of the record's rows (r3–r32) are method-comparison points at a fixed 30M size and are relinked to none. The scaling-law evidence rests on the BF16 baseline fit and figure-only extrapolation. A label of uses_without_test/T4 would also be defensible, since scaling laws are chiefly used as a comparison tool.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies quantization-dependent scaling on C4 and reports a baseline fit plus loss sweeps at fixed 30M parameters. It does not independently test the original claim across several orders of magnitude in parameters, tokens, and compute for ordinary full-precision language-model training.
The paper shows scaling-law fits alongside larger-model points, but does not give exact numerical predicted-versus-observed losses for each extrapolated run.
The paper analyzes compute-budget choices of forward/backward precision, not the loss-minimising parameter-count/token-count allocation as a function of compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text pretraining on C4; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes are not tested.

The paper reports consistency between C4 validation loss and three few-shot benchmarks for tested Llama models, but does not establish downstream predictability across task types or model families generally.

The paper fits alternative functional forms, but does not test whether published parameter/token exponents or compute-optimal allocations disagree because of parameter counting, schedules, data, or fitting choices, nor whether loss curves systematically bend away from power laws.

relation.reason: Its baseline loss-law fits and downstream evaluations bear on V1 and V6, beyond using scaling laws to compare training methods.

tranche.reason: The study fits and compares precision-dependent loss laws and reports baseline fit errors and downstream correspondence, supplying its own evidence on the claim.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v4, dated 15 Jan 2026. The baseline law includes an outer exponent γ; Figure 5's caption says 30–200M parameters, conflicting with the accompanying text's 100M–1.6B.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: C4 pretraining with Quartet at 30M parameters across D/N = 25× to 400×, and the reported BF16 baseline fit
reader_labels.reason: The baseline is fit with a parameter/data scaling law, and Quartet's validation loss declines across the reported data-ratio sweep (r1, r3–r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Alternative fully quantized methods at 30M parameters
reader_labels.reason: The loss curves vary substantially by method; LUQ–FP4 is nearly flat, several methods have poor losses, and LSS–INT4 has NaNs at multiple data ratios, so the observed scaling behavior is not uniform across setups (r8–r32).
